text: On-call rotations get designed once, by default, and then left alone for years — one week, one primary, no pay, repeat. This lesson is about three decisions that are easy to get wrong that way: how long a rotation should run, who backs up the primary when they can't respond, and why compensation isn't a perk, it's part of how reliably your team handles the next real incident.

Rotation length is a trade-off, not a default. A full week means a bad stretch of pages compounds longer before relief arrives; a shorter three-to-four day rotation caps that exposure at the cost of more frequent handoffs. A real secondary matters just as much — if the primary doesn't acknowledge a page, it needs to escalate automatically, not depend on someone noticing in Slack. And paying for on-call, through a stipend, per-page pay, or comp time, changes real behavior: uncompensated on-call quietly pushes engineers toward muting alerts or rushing a fix just to get back to sleep.

Here's what that escalation actually looks like configured, not promised. The primary gets paged first, with a defined window — commonly five minutes — to acknowledge. No acknowledgment, and the secondary gets paged automatically. Still nothing, and it escalates again, to a manager or lead. That's configuration in your paging tool, with a real timeout, not a hope that someone's keeping half an eye on the channel.

Now the part that gets missed: burnout isn't just unpleasant for the engineer carrying the pager, it measurably degrades how well incidents get handled. A fatigued responder takes longer to build an accurate picture of what's actually broken. They're more likely to apply a fix that treats the symptom in front of them instead of the real cause. And the judgment calls that matter most — when to escalate, when to roll back instead of patch forward — are exactly the calls exhaustion erodes first.

A rotation with the right length, a real secondary, and fair compensation gets you a sustainable team. It doesn't automatically get you a runbook anyone can actually follow at 3 A.M. — that's next: what makes a runbook survive real incident pressure instead of getting skipped in favor of improvising from memory.
